doc.title: Carl Allen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, Georgia, January 4, 2013

title: Explaining the triplet feel, and Mulgrew Miller on singing and dancing
summary: Allen explains swing as triple versus duple feel and says the music's loss of dancability is the real problem, quoting Mulgrew Miller.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: And I just want to, as an aside, you use the word triplet with your students to define the swinging eighth note — the first two notes tied together. Do you verbalize that to them? How would you verbalize that to them?

Well it’s a triple feel versus a duple feel. You know, [scats rhythm] as opposed to [scats]. So that opens up a whole other thing — it can be Latin, straight eighth, funk, R&B, so, a lot of other things. The triplet is hard man. The triplet is hard to deal with. But I think what’s killed the music is not so much the standards. In my opinion it’s more it’s losing its dancability. A great friend a mine, a pianist, said something so hip I wish I had come up with it. And if he wasn’t such a great friend I’d probably say I came up with it and wouldn’t give him credit. But since he’s such a great friend I have to give him credit. Mulgrew Miller says, “The music is supposed to be singing and dancing all the time.” This music is supposed to be singing and dancing all the time. And I agree with that. When you think about great jazz music, it’s singing and dancing. The melodies are singing and the rhythms are dancing. And it’s infectious in that you can’t sit still.
